title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a system trained on copyrighted material without securing licenses from the rights holders before deployment. Udio, an AI music generation service that produces songs from text prompts, allegedly used recordings it had no permission to use as training data. This is a data-sourcing failure that preceded any user interaction, meaning it was built into the system before a single song was generated for a customer.

The failure would have required legal review of training data provenance at the model-building stage to catch. That review apparently did not happen, or did not result in licensed agreements, before the product launched. Multiple major rights holders pursued separate legal actions, and a class action from independent artists was also allowed to proceed, suggesting the alleged unlicensed use was not limited to a narrow set of recordings.

None of the lawsuits have produced final verdicts, and the allegations of copying are not established findings of fact. The settlements reached with some labels resolve those specific claims without constituting judicial rulings on liability. Whether the new licensed platform resolves the underlying disputes with remaining plaintiffs is not established.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve claims that Udio used copyrighted music to train its artificial intelligence system. The company will launch a new platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. UMG's CEO stated the settlement demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists and songwriters while embracing new technologies and business models. The financial terms were not disclosed.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, allows users to generate original songs with AI by providing text prompts. The lawsuit had alleged that Udio used songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar compositions without permission or compensation. This marks Udio's first licensing deal with a major music label. The company stated that artists can opt into the new platform and will receive compensation, though specific details were not provided. UMG simultaneously announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
